strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and timely problem: reference-based transfer of temporally evolving visual effects, which is distinct from standard text-only video editing, static style transfer, or keyframe-conditioned generation.

The proposed dataset construction is ambitious and practically valuable, combining LoRA-based I2V effects, an automated neural V2V pair-generation pipeline, and programmatic temporal effects to produce over 120K triplets across many effect types.

The method is conceptually simple and plausible: extending a strong Wan video backbone with reference-video and input-video conditioning via latent concatenation is a reasonable design for feed-forward effect transfer.
Qualitative examples and the user study suggest that reference conditioning can capture temporal cues that prompt-only baselines miss, especially for effects that are hard to describe textually.

The paper includes useful implementation details, validation on unseen effects, controllable guidance for balancing input/reference adherence, and a candid limitations section discussing occlusion failures, domain bias, and compute cost.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is weaker than the claims. Most baselines are prompt-only or condition on pose/depth rather than on a reference video, so the comparisons partly demonstrate that reference information is useful rather than isolating the merit of the proposed architecture or dataset.

Quantitative metrics are only loose proxies. VideoPrism/CLIP similarity to the reference can conflate content, style, and motion, while input similarity can reward under-editing. The paper acknowledges this but does not provide a stronger task-specific metric or ground-truth evaluation.

The user study is important but under-specified in the main paper: details on annotator pool, randomization, statistical significance, per-effect breakdowns, failure cases, and possible prompt/reference bias are limited, making it hard to judge robustness of the reported win rates.

The validation data are not fully independent in spirit. Neural V2V validation uses the same generation pipeline with novel prompts, and code-based validation shares operation/transition families with training, so generalization to genuinely new real-world effects remains uncertain.

The technical novelty of the model itself is moderate. The main architectural change is latent/reference concatenation on top of a strong pretrained Wan model with LoRA fine-tuning; the larger contribution is the task/data pipeline rather than a fundamentally new modeling approach.

Dataset provenance and reproducibility need more care. The work relies on open-source LoRAs, generated images/videos, Senorita masks, GPT-4o-generated prompts, and large proprietary or rapidly changing foundation models; licensing, filtering criteria, release plan, and exact prompt/configuration details are not sufficiently clear for reproducing the benchmark.

Important ablations are missing or only lightly covered, such as training with each data source removed, reference-token design alternatives, effect-category-level performance, sensitivity to reference/input mismatch, and comparisons to adapted reference-based personalization or dynamic-concept methods.

The method is computationally expensive, roughly doubling inference time and token count, and the paper does not deeply analyze memory limits, resolution/length scaling, or whether the approach remains practical beyond 33 frames at 480p.

strengths: The paper tackles a compelling and underexplored problem: transferring temporally evolving visual effects from a reference video to a different image/video in a feed-forward setting. This is a useful interface for video editing because many effects are hard to specify with text alone.

The proposed triplet formulation is intuitive, and the dataset construction combines several complementary sources: LoRA-generated I2V effects, model-generated V2V pairs, and programmatic temporal effects. The claimed scale of 120K triplets and 1,700 effects could be valuable if released with sufficient metadata and quality controls.
The architecture is a plausible extension of a strong video diffusion backbone, and the guidance formulation for trading off reference adherence and input preservation is practically relevant.

The paper includes qualitative comparisons, embedding-based metrics, and a human preference study. The user study suggests that viewers often prefer the proposed method over text-only baselines for reference adherence.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not strong enough for the breadth of the claims. The validation sets have no ground-truth transferred outputs, so the quantitative evidence relies on VideoPrism/CLIP similarity to reference and input videos, which are weak proxies for correct temporal effect transfer.

The baselines are not fully convincing. Since most compared systems cannot use a reference video, the experiments mainly show the advantage of having extra reference information rather than isolating the contribution of the proposed architecture or training recipe.

The dataset contribution is hard to assess because most data are synthetic outputs from existing generative models or hand-coded effects. The paper gives limited evidence of data quality, filtering criteria, leakage controls, or diversity beyond effect lists.

Claims of generalization are overstated. For code-based effects, held-out examples appear to share the same operation families and differ largely in hyperparameters; the broader V2V pipeline is also heavily human-centric and generated-model-centric.

The user study is under-specified despite being the main evidence: details on annotators, unique examples, randomization, statistical uncertainty, quality controls, and separation of reference adherence from general visual appeal are insufficient.

Ablations are thin. The paper does not systematically analyze dataset sources, architecture choices, reference concatenation strategy, guidance terms, or training mixture, making it unclear which components drive the gains.

Reproducibility is limited because the method depends on large video models, generated datasets, online LoRAs, GPT-4o-generated prompts, and manually curated effect code/configurations, with only a promise of code release.

The writing is understandable but sometimes imprecise and overclaims novelty and temporal coherence relative to the evidence. Overall, the idea is interesting, but the scientific case is not yet convincing enough for acceptance.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and underexplored problem: transferring temporally evolving visual effects from a reference video to a target image or video. The task is clearly motivated, practically useful, and distinct from standard text-only video editing, static reference conditioning, or first/last-frame control.

A major strength is the dataset contribution. The authors propose a large-scale triplet construction strategy with over 120K triplets and more than 1,700 effects, combining LoRA-based I2V effects, an automated V2V generation pipeline, and programmatic temporal effects. This is a credible and useful way to bootstrap supervision for a task where naturally paired data is scarce.

The method is technically sound and pragmatic. Extending a strong Wan-based video diffusion backbone with reference-video and input-video conditioning is not conceptually radical, but it is well aligned with the task and appears to work effectively in a feed-forward, tuning-free setting.

The qualitative results are compelling. The shown examples demonstrate that RefVFX captures dynamic cues such as camera motion, material transformation, occlusion-like interactions, and temporal stylization better than prompt-only or control-based baselines.

The human preference study is a meaningful evaluation choice for this task. Since reference-effect transfer is difficult to capture with a single automatic metric, the reported pairwise preferences across I2V, neural V2V, and code-based effects provide useful evidence that users prefer the proposed outputs, especially for reference adherence.

The paper is generally clear, with well-organized explanations of the data sources, generation pipeline, architecture, evaluation settings, and limitations. The supplement gives useful implementation and dataset details, including effect lists, hyperparameters, runtime, and known failure modes.
weaknesses: The technical novelty of the model itself is moderate. Much of the contribution comes from dataset construction and conditioning design around an existing large video backbone, rather than a fundamentally new modeling mechanism. This is acceptable for an applied/systems-style contribution, but the paper should frame the novelty more explicitly around the task, data, and system rather than implying a major algorithmic advance.

The evaluation is somewhat constrained by the lack of truly reference-conditioned baselines. Most baselines receive only text descriptions of the reference effect, so the comparison partly demonstrates that text is an insufficient interface rather than isolating the benefit of the proposed architecture against alternative reference-video conditioning designs.

The automatic metrics are only weak proxies for task success. VideoPrism reference similarity and CLIP/frame similarity do not reliably disentangle effect transfer, content preservation, motion preservation, and possible copying from the reference. The paper acknowledges this, but the quantitative evidence remains limited.

More ablations would strengthen the scientific case. The paper includes a no-reference comparison and guidance visualization, but it would be useful to quantify the contribution of the three dataset sources, the reference concatenation design, mask choices, LoRA fine-tuning choices, and training-data scale.

The dataset generation pipeline depends heavily on synthetic/generated data from strong proprietary or rapidly evolving models and open LoRA collections. This raises reproducibility and attribution concerns unless the released code/data clearly documents exact model versions, licenses, filtering procedures, and whether all training triplets can be redistributed.

The validation sets are relatively small and partly close to the training generation mechanisms. Code-based test effects share operation families with training, and the neural V2V validation is generated by the authors' own pipeline. Stronger evidence on real user-provided reference videos, out-of-domain scenes, non-human-centric settings, and environmental or abstract effects would better support broad generalization claims.

The method is computationally expensive: about seven minutes per 33-frame 480p video on an A100, roughly twice the baseline inference cost. This is acceptable for research, but it limits interactive use and should temper claims about practical usability.

Some limitations visible in the paper, such as difficulty with complete occlusions and complex physical interactions, are important for visual effects transfer. The current model may imitate the appearance of an effect without consistently preserving its underlying spatial or causal behavior.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and timely problem: transferring temporally evolving visual effects from a reference video to a target image/video, which is a meaningful extension beyond text-only video editing and static reference conditioning.

The proposed dataset construction is ambitious and practically valuable, combining LoRA-based I2V effects, a generated V2V pipeline, and programmatic temporal effects to obtain over 120K triplets and many effect categories.

The method is technically plausible and well aligned with modern video diffusion practice: extending Wan-style conditioning with input-video and reference-video latents is simple, scalable, and supports feed-forward inference without per-effect tuning.
Qualitative examples show clear cases where prompt-only baselines fail to capture temporal effects while RefVFX better follows the reference dynamics and preserves input content.

The user study is a suitable primary evaluation for this subjective task, includes several baselines and dimensions, and reports consistent preference for the proposed method across I2V, neural V2V, and code-based V2V settings.
The paper includes useful implementation details, ablation via a no-reference variant, controllable guidance analysis, runtime reporting, and an explicit limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is relatively limited: the main modeling change is latent concatenation/reference conditioning on top of a strong existing Wan backbone, so much of the contribution rests on data generation and engineering rather than a fundamentally new algorithm.

The evaluation is not fully convincing. The validation set is small, with only over 100 V2V instances, and the paper relies heavily on qualitative examples and 2AFC preferences; there is no ground-truth test set or task-specific metric that cleanly measures successful effect transfer.

The baselines are at an inherent disadvantage because they receive textual descriptions rather than the reference video signal. This supports the value of reference conditioning, but makes it hard to isolate whether RefVFX is better than alternative ways of using visual references or stronger adaptation/personalization methods.

The quantitative metrics are weak proxies. VideoPrism/CLIP similarities can conflate style, content, and motion, and the VBench metrics in the appendix show comparable or sometimes worse aesthetics/dynamics than baselines, limiting the strength of the quantitative evidence.

Dataset quality and generalization remain concerns. Much of the training data is synthetic or generated by other foundation models, the V2V pipeline may imprint biases/artifacts from Qwen/Wan/VACE, and the paper notes a human-centric/foreground-dominant bias that may limit broader cinematic or environmental effects.

Reproducibility and attribution details are incomplete for a dataset/benchmark-style contribution: code and data are only promised after publication, prompts are often paraphrased rather than fully specified, and licensing/redistribution implications for scraped/open LoRAs, generated data, and Senorita-derived masks are not deeply discussed.

The user-study reporting would benefit from more detail on exact sample counts per baseline/criterion, annotator filtering beyond practice trials, significance testing for close comparisons such as IVA, and whether repeated trials/videos create dependence not captured by the bootstrap procedure.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and underexplored problem: transferring time-varying visual effects from a reference video to a target image/video. This is a relevant direction for controllable video generation beyond text prompts and static conditioning.

The authors make a serious data-engineering effort, combining LoRA-based I2V effects, a generated V2V pipeline, and programmatic temporal effects into a claimed 120K-triplet dataset covering 1,700 effects. The triplet construction is a reasonable way to formulate reference-conditioned effect transfer.

The system is practically motivated and feed-forward at inference time. The conditioning design built on Wan2.1 is simple and scalable, and the paper reports human-preference studies across I2V, neural V2V, and code-based V2V settings.
The manuscript includes useful limitations, implementation details, examples of controllable guidance, and some appendix documentation of datasets, prompts, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited. The model appears to be mainly a width/latent concatenation conditioning adaptation of an existing Wan2.1 FLF2V model with LoRA fine-tuning. The main contribution is therefore closer to an applied/systems plus dataset paper than an algorithms paper, but the evidence is not strong enough for the broad claims made about a new benchmark and first systematic study.

The dataset construction raises major validity concerns. A large fraction of the training data is synthetic, generated by chains of existing image/video models and programmatic filters. This may teach the model to imitate artifacts of the data-generation pipeline rather than genuine reference-effect transfer. The paper does not provide enough independent validation of triplet quality, failure rates, filtering criteria, diversity, or leakage between generated training/evaluation distributions.

The evaluation is weak for the strength of the claims. The validation set is described as only “over 100” V2V instances, with generated and manually filtered examples. This is small and potentially biased for a video generation paper claiming broad generalization across complex unseen effects.

The baselines are not fully comparable. Since existing baselines cannot use the reference video, they receive text descriptions instead, which puts them at an inherent disadvantage on a task defined around visual reference conditioning. This comparison shows that reference conditioning helps, but not that the proposed architecture or dataset is the right or best way to do the task.

The quantitative metrics are only loose proxies. VideoPrism/CLIP similarities to input and reference videos do not disentangle effect transfer from content, style, identity, or under-editing, and the authors themselves acknowledge that metrics only partially reflect the task. In Table 3/4, input similarity often drops for the proposed method, and the gains in reference similarity are modest in some settings.

The user study reports win rates mostly in the 53-67% range, which is supportive but not decisive given the subjective task, possible presentation bias, and unclear sampling over effects/videos. Details such as exact number of trials per comparison, annotator qualification, inter-annotator agreement, and whether generated failures were included are insufficient for a primary-evidence claim.

Important ablations are missing or underdeveloped. The paper does not convincingly isolate the contributions of each dataset source, the reference-video conditioning mechanism, training scale, LoRA fine-tuning choice, text conditioning, guidance terms, or last-frame retention. The “No Ref” baseline is useful but not enough to establish why the proposed design works.

Reproducibility is uncertain. The paper says code will be released, but the method depends on many external generative models, open-source LoRAs, generated prompts, manual filtering, and large compute. Dataset licensing/attribution and redistributability are not adequately discussed, especially for Hugging Face LoRAs, Senorita-derived videos/masks, and model-generated data.

The paper overclaims. Phrases such as “unprecedented diversity,” “first systematic study,” and “establishing a new benchmark” are not backed by a public benchmark protocol, ground-truth held-out set, clear task metrics, or strong comparisons to reference-capable alternatives/customization methods.

Qualitative results are visually suggestive but too selective. The paper relies heavily on a few examples, while the stated limitations indicate failures on occlusion and complex interactions; these are central to many claimed temporal effects rather than minor corner cases.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and useful problem: reference-based transfer of temporally evolving visual effects, a setting that is not well served by prompt-only or static-conditioning video editing systems. The task formulation is clear and relevant to computer vision and generative video editing.

The main contribution is practically meaningful: a large triplet dataset spanning LoRA-based I2V effects, neural V2V effects, and programmatic temporal effects. The data construction pipeline is creative and appears scalable, especially the pairing strategy that uses two examples of the same effect to teach effect transfer rather than content copying.

The method is technically sensible and well integrated with a strong video diffusion backbone. The conditioning design that combines input video latents, reference video latents, text, and classifier-free guidance directions is simple but appropriate, and the feed-forward inference setting is attractive compared with per-effect optimization or per-reference finetuning.

The evaluation covers I2V, neural V2V, and code-based V2V settings, including unseen effect categories. The user study is especially important for this problem, where available automatic metrics are weak proxies; reported preferences consistently favor the proposed method across reference adherence and overall match.

Qualitative examples support the central claim that reference video conditioning captures temporal behaviors that text-only baselines miss, such as staged transformations, camera/effect rhythm, and evolving occlusions. The appendix also gives useful implementation details, dataset categories, user-study protocol, and limitations.
weaknesses: The automatic quantitative evidence is limited. Similarity to the reference and input via VideoPrism/CLIP is only a rough proxy and can confound desired effect transfer with content leakage or under-editing. The paper acknowledges this, but the scientific case still relies heavily on subjective comparisons and qualitative examples.

The baseline comparison is somewhat asymmetric because existing baselines do not receive reference video conditioning. This is understandable given the novelty of the task, but the paper would be stronger with additional adapted baselines, such as naive reference-token conditioning, retrieval/prompt expansion from the reference, frame/style transfer variants, or stronger ablations of the proposed conditioning design.

Ablations are relatively thin for a paper whose contribution mixes dataset, architecture, and guidance. The No Ref ablation helps, but there is little isolation of the three data sources, width-wise latent concatenation choice, reference/input dropout strategy, guidance components, or training scale. This makes it hard to know which ingredients are most responsible for the gains.

The dataset is large and useful, but much of it is synthetic and derived from existing generative models, public LoRAs, and generated prompts. The paper should more carefully discuss data licensing/attribution, possible biases inherited from these sources, and whether the benchmark may favor the same model family used to generate or train the data.

The validation sets are fairly small in places: 28 unseen I2V effects and a little over 100 V2V instances. While the user study has many annotations, broader evaluation across non-human-centric scenes, real-world footage, longer videos, and more diverse environmental/cinematic effects would better support claims of generalization.

The method is computationally expensive, roughly doubling inference time to about 7 minutes per 33-frame 480p video on an A100. This does not undermine the contribution, but it limits practical deployment and should be weighed against the feed-forward efficiency claim.

Some limitations are important for the claimed task: the model can fail on fine-grained occlusion, complex interactions, and scenes outside the human/foreground-centric training distribution. These are central cases for visual effects transfer, so the current system is not yet fully robust, although the limitations are clearly stated.
